content: Many individuals diagnosed with bipolar disorder require long-term treatment to prevent the recurrence of mood episodes. Antipsychotic medications, such as olanzapine, are frequently used to manage acute manic episodes. It is essential to determine whether olanzapine can play a role in the long-term prevention of manic, depressive, and mixed episodes in this population. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of olanzapine, either as a standalone treatment or in combination with other therapies, in preventing the recurrence of mood episodes in patients with bipolar disorder. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Collaboration Depression, Anxiety and Neurosis Controlled Trials Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO, covering studies up to 2007. Experts, trial investigators, and pharmaceutical companies were also contacted to identify additional relevant data. The analysis included randomized controlled trials comparing olanzapine with placebo or other active treatments for long-term management of bipolar disorder. Five trials, involving a total of 1,165 participants, were included in the review. When comparing olanzapine to placebo (either alone or in combination with lithium or valproate), there was no statistically significant difference in the number of participants who experienced a relapse into a mood episode (relative risk [RR] 0.68, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.43 to 1.07, p = 0.09; based on two studies with 460 participants). However, when the analysis was restricted to a trial comparing olanzapine monotherapy to placebo, a statistically significant benefit was observed in favor of olanzapine (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.69, p < 0.00001). When comparing olanzapine to other mood stabilizers, such as lithium or valproate, no statistically significant difference was found in preventing symptomatic relapse for any type of mood episode. However, olanzapine demonstrated greater efficacy than lithium in preventing symptomatic manic relapses (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.89, p = 0.01; based on one study with 361 participants). Olanzapine, whether used alone or as an adjunctive treatment with mood stabilizers, was associated with significantly greater weight gain compared to placebo. Additionally, while olanzapine was linked to a lower rate of manic worsening, it was associated with a higher rate of weight gain and depressive symptoms compared to lithium. In conclusion, although the evidence is limited, olanzapine appears to be effective in preventing further mood episodes in patients who have previously responded to olanzapine during an initial manic or mixed episode and who have not achieved satisfactory results with lithium or valproate. Despite these findings, the current body of evidence supports lithium as the first-line maintenance treatment for bipolar disorder.
